segments.translit:
śrīmatsatguruvaktrapaṅkajarasāsvādasphuraddhīdayo
natvā śrīkuliśeśamaddvayadhiyaṃ śraddhāprasannānanaḥ|
śrīlūyīcaraṇādisiddharacite'pyāścaryyacaryyācaye
sadvartmāvagamāya nirmmalagirāṃ ṭīkāṃ vidhāsye sphuṭam||
segments.translation: My wisdom and compassion shining from tasting the nectar of the lotus mouth of the glorious true [guru]{guru}, my face serene with faith, I bow to the glorious Lord of the [vajra]{vajra}, whose understanding is nondual; and on the wondrous collection of songs of [conduct]{carya} composed by the [siddhas]{siddha}, beginning with the venerable [Lūyī]{p-luyi}, I will clearly compose a commentary on their stainless words, so that the true path may be understood.
segments.note: Munidatta opens with his own verse of homage. Having tasted the nectar of the true [guru]{guru}'s lotus mouth and bowed to the Lord of the [vajra]{vajra}, he promises a clear commentary on the stainless words of the wondrous songs of [conduct]{carya} composed by the [siddhas]{siddha}, [Lūyī]{p-luyi} first among them, so that the true path may be understood.

flags.note: -dhīdayo is taken as dhī + dayā, 'wisdom and compassion'. The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has rab gsal brtse ba'i thugs, 'a mind brightly shining with love', which confirms dayā; it construes the compound as 'a mind shining with compassion', a possible alternative to my 'wisdom and compassion shining'. A reading dhī + udaya would normally give -dhyudaya and is set aside.

advayadhiyam is taken with the Lord of the vajra, 'whose understanding is nondual'; the Tibetan (gnyis med blo ldan dpal ldan rdo rje'i dbang phyug) construes it the same way. Apposition ('the Lord of the vajra, nondual understanding itself') remains possible.

nirmmalagirāṃ (genitive plural), revised: I now take it as governed by ṭīkāṃ, 'a commentary on their (the songs') stainless words', the usual construction with ṭīkā; the previous draft had 'in stainless words'. The Tibetan (lam mchog dri ma med pa'i tshig ni rtogs par bya phyir, 'so that the stainless words of the supreme path may be understood') likewise treats the stainless words as what is to be understood, not as the style of the commentary, though it joins them to the path. 'Of stainless speech', describing the siddhas, is a third possibility. The particle 'pi after racite looks metrical and is not translated.

śraddhāprasannānanaḥ is nominative and describes the speaker ('my face serene with faith'). The Tibetan gives the Lord a 'stainless face' (dri med zhal mnga') and makes faith the manner of the bow (dad pas phyag 'tshal nas); the Sanskrit case does not allow that, so I keep the printed construal. Tibetan renderings that do not change the reading: siddha is grub pa (not the glossary's grub thob), and glu, 'song', is added in spyod pa'i glu yi tshogs, which supports 'songs of conduct' for caryācaya.

segments.translit:
rāgapaṭamañjarī—kāātaruvaretyādi| śrīmadgurucaraṇāravindamakarandavindusandohaśāntasantarpitānandastimitahṛ[da]yaḥ satyadvayamahāmohabhramajaladhimadhyanimagnā'śaraṇadīnajanasamuddharaṇakāmo hi siddhācāryya [2] śrīlūipādaḥ praṇidhipreritāvatāraṇārthaṃ kāataruvyājena suddhadharmmatāpīṭhikāṃ prākṛ[ta]bhāsayā racayitumāha kāyetyādi| rūpādayaḥ pañcaskandhāḥ| ṣaḍindriyāṇi dhātavo viṣayāśca grāhyagrāhakagrahaṇopalakṣitapallavatvāt kāyataruvaratvena gṛhītaḥ| nanvacetanatvāt kathaṃ kāyastaruvaraḥ| naiṣa doṣaḥ|
tathaiva bahiśāstrakārairapyutprekṣālaṅkāraparaiḥ kiñcid bhedādhiṣṭhānaṃ hi sādṛśyamudīritaṃ| kimutāsya prakṛtyābhāṣadoṣavaśāt cāñcalyatayā prākṛtasattvenācyutirūpo hi rāhuḥ| sa eva kālaḥ| kṛṣṇapratipaddaśāyāṃ praviṣṭaḥ| yasmāt nandābhadrājayāriktāpūrṇātithikrameṇa saṃvṛttibodhicittamṛgāṅkaṃ śoṣaṃ nayatīti| ayamatyarthaṃ kṛṣṇācāryyapādairabhihitaḥ
varagiri-kandara-guhira jagu saela citta ṭṭai|
vimala-salila śoṣa yāiya kālagni paiṭai|
tathāca rativajre—
patite bodhicitte tu sarvvasiddhinidhānake|
mūrcchite skandhavijñāne kutaḥ si[2ka]ddhiraninditā||
tathāca sampuṭodbhavatantrarāje—
analpasaṃkalpatamobhibhūtaṃ
prabhañjanonmattataḍiccalañca|
rāgādidurvvāramalāvaliptaṃ
cittaṃ hi saṃsāramuvāca vajrī||
tasmāt ye kecit prādeśikāḥ paripakvakuśalāḥ bhagavataḥ pañcakramapraveśopāyadhāraṇapūrvveṇa yuganaddharūpaṃ sahajānandaphalaṃ satatamanveṣayanti te'pi vajropa[ma]samādhiṃ sākṣāt kurvvanti| āryyadevapādairapyuktaṃ pañcakramānupūrvveṇa vinā niṣpannakramasambodhi[ṃ] sākṣātkarttuṃ na prāpyate|
segments.translation:
[Rāga]{raga} [Paṭamañjarī]{patamanjari}. 'The body is a [fine tree]{taruvara}', and so on. His heart soothed and sated by the flood of nectar drops from the lotus feet of his glorious [guru]{guru}, and steeped in [joy]{ananda}, and longing to rescue the helpless and wretched people sunk in the middle of the ocean of confusion and great delusion about the [two truths]{satyadvaya}, the [siddha]{siddha} master, the venerable [Lūyī]{p-luyi}, says 'The body', and so on, in order to lead them in as his vow impelled him, and to compose in the vernacular, under the guise of a body-tree, the groundwork of the pure nature of reality. The five [aggregates]{skandha}, beginning with form. The six senses, the elements and the [sense objects]{visaya} are taken as the [fine tree]{taruvara} of the body, because its leaves are marked by [the grasped and the grasper]{grahya-grahaka} and by grasping. But a tree is insentient: how can the body be a [fine tree]{taruvara}? That is no fault.
For in just this way even the authors of outside treatises, devoted to the figure of speech called utprekṣā, have declared that likeness rests on some difference. And what of its restlessness? Through restlessness under the sway of the fault of the natural [appearances]{abhasa}, [Rāhu]{p-rahu}, for an ordinary being, has the form of falling. He is [Death]{kala}. He has entered at the first lunar day of the dark fortnight, for through the sequence of the lunar days Nandā, Bhadrā, Jayā, Riktā and Pūrṇā he brings the [moon]{moon} of [conventional]{samvrti} [bodhicitta]{bodhicitta} to drying up. The venerable master [Kāṇha]{p-kanha} has spoken of him expressly:
In the deep cave of the great mountain the whole world, the [mind]{citta}, breaks;
the pure water dries away; the fire of time enters.
And so in the [Rativajra]{tx-rativajra}:
When [bodhicitta]{bodhicitta}, the treasury of all [accomplishments]{siddhi}, has fallen
and the consciousness of the [aggregates]{skandha} has swooned, where can blameless [accomplishment]{siddhi} come from?
And so in the king of tantras, the [Sampuṭodbhava]{tx-samputa}:
Overcome by the darkness of countless concepts,
restless as lightning driven wild by the storm wind,
smeared with the stubborn stains of passion and the rest:
the [mind]{citta} itself, said the holder of the [vajra]{vajra}, is [saṃsāra]{samsara}.
Therefore, whoever among those of limited scope have ripened roots of virtue and, first taking up the means of entering the [Blessed One]{p-bhagavat}'s [five stages]{pancakrama}, constantly seek the fruit, [innate joy]{sahajananda}, whose form is [coupled union]{yuganaddha}: they too directly realize the [vajra]{vajra}-like [samādhi]{samadhi}. The venerable [Āryadeva]{p-aryadeva} too has said: 'Without the [five stages]{pancakrama} in their order, one cannot come to realize directly the awakening of the [completion stage]{nispannakrama}.'
segments.note: Munidatta takes senses, elements and objects as the body-tree, naming the five [aggregates]{skandha}, evidently as its branches. The mind is restless through the fault of natural appearances; [Death]{kala} is [Rāhu]{p-rahu}, in an ordinary being the form of falling, who from the dark fortnight's first day dries up the [moon]{moon} of [conventional]{samvrti} [bodhicitta]{bodhicitta}. [Innate joy]{sahajananda} comes through the [five stages]{pancakrama}.

equations.en: the five aggregates, beginning with form (implied by juxtaposition; Munidatta does not say 'branches')
the six senses, the elements and the sense objects, taken as the fine tree of the body, its leaves marked by the grasped, the grasper and grasping
Rāhu, who for an ordinary being has the form of falling, and who has entered on the first lunar day of the dark fortnight
conventional bodhicitta, pictured as the moon that Rāhu dries up

citations.quoted: varagiri-kandara-guhira jagu saela citta ṭṭai … (In the deep cave of the great mountain …)
citations.work: Kṛṣṇācārya (Kāṇha), an Apabhraṃśa verse; perhaps from his Dohākoṣa

citations.quoted: patite bodhicitte tu sarvvasiddhinidhānake … (When bodhicitta … has fallen …)
citations.work: Rativajra (so named by Munidatta; the work is not otherwise identified)

citations.quoted: analpasaṃkalpatamobhibhūtaṃ … (Overcome by the darkness of countless concepts …)
citations.work: Sampuṭodbhava, 'king of tantras' (probably the Saṃpuṭa Tantra)

citations.quoted: pañcakramānupūrvveṇa vinā niṣpannakramasambodhiṃ … (Without the five stages in their order …)
citations.work: Āryadeva (work not named; perhaps the Caryāmelāpakapradīpa)

flags.note: prākṛtasattvenācyutirūpo hi rāhuḥ: as printed, acyuti- 'not falling, imperishable' gives little sense. I read cyuti- 'falling' (the loss of bodhicitta), and the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) now supports this: tha mal pa'i sems 'dzag pa'i rang bzhin gyis sgra gcan, 'Rāhu, by the nature of the leaking of the ordinary mind', with no negative. prākṛtasattvena is taken as 'for an ordinary being' (the Tibetan: 'of the ordinary mind').

kimutāsya, revised: kimuta normally means 'how much more', and the previous draft joined the sentence to the argument about likeness ('All the more so in its case…'). The Tibetan renders it as a question, ci'i phyir brtags na … g.yo ba de yis so, 'if one asks why: because of its moving…', which makes the sentence a comment on 'restless' in line 1b. I now follow that segmentation ('And what of its restlessness?'). The Sanskrit remains loose and may be corrupt.

prakṛtyābhāṣa: the Tibetan rang bzhin du snang ba, 'appearing as (its) nature', confirms ābhāsa 'appearance' rather than ābhāṣa 'speech' (the scribe interchanges s and ṣ). Probably the tantric pair of 'natural states' (prakṛti) and 'appearances' (ābhāsa); rendered 'the natural appearances' and linked to abhasa. A more technical rendering may be wanted.

prākṛ[ta]bhāsayā, 'in the vernacular', rests on Shastri's restoration of a damaged syllable. The Tibetan has instead dgongs pa'i tshig gis, 'in intentional (twilight) language', and renders the phrase around it as rnam par dag pa'i chos nyid gzhi'i rang bzhin gyi snang ba, 'the appearance of the nature of the ground, pure reality', apparently reading prakṛti-ābhāsa. I translate Shastri's text, but his restoration should be treated as uncertain.

suddhadharmmatāpīṭhikāṃ, revised: pīṭhikā can mean 'introduction, preface' (the previous draft's choice) or 'seat, pedestal, base'. The Tibetan gzhi, 'ground, basis', favours the second, which would also anticipate the seat of the last couplet. I now render 'the groundwork', to keep both senses open; 'a seat for the pure nature of reality' is the more literal alternative.

sa eva kālaḥ: the Sanskrit nominative identifies Rāhu with the song's kāla ('He is Death'), and praviṣṭaḥ echoes the song's paiṭho. The Tibetan instead has de nyid kyi dus su, 'at that very time', reading kāla as time and joining it to the entry on the first lunar day; it also renders kālāgni in Kāṇha's verse as dus kyi me, 'fire of time'. Yet its own song line 1b names Rāhu (sgra gcan) as what enters the restless mind. I keep the identification.

Kāṇha's Apabhraṃśa couplet, first line: 'citta ṭṭai' is damaged (perhaps cittu tuṭṭai, 'the mind breaks'). The Tibetan has 'gro rnams ma lus kun chad gyur, 'all beings without exception are cut off', with no word for mind, which suggests the verb was a form of tuṭṭ- 'break, be cut' and leaves citta doubtful. I keep the printed 'mind', in apposition to 'the whole world', tentatively. Second line: the Tibetan (dri med chu rgyun skams nas 'gro/ dus kyi me ni rab tu 'jug) has two coordinate clauses, so I have dropped my earlier 'when' and render 'the pure water dries away; the fire of time enters' (yāiya taken as jāi, 'goes').

rūpādayaḥ pañcaskandhāḥ stands alone and evidently glosses the five branches, though Munidatta does not say 'branches'. The Tibetan has gzugs la sogs pa'i phung po rnams, without 'five', and runs the aggregates into the next sentence, so that aggregates, senses, elements and objects together are 'taken as the fine body-tree', indicated as like leaves because they are grasped as grasped and grasper. The equation of branches with aggregates is therefore less secure than the glossary entry taruvara suggests.

nanvacetanatvāt: 'since (a tree) is insentient'. The Tibetan has sems dang ldan pa'i phyir, 'since it is sentient', of the body (as if sacetanatvāt); the objection is the same either way. gṛhītaḥ is masculine singular although its subjects are plural; the body (kāyaḥ) seems to be understood.

bhagavataḥ: I take it with pañcakrama, 'the Blessed One's five stages'. The Tibetan construes it with paripakvakuśalāḥ, bcom ldan 'das kyis dge ba rnams yongs su smin pa, 'whose virtues the Blessed One has ripened', and does not call the five stages the Blessed One's. Both construals are possible; the glossary entries p-bhagavat and pancakrama currently follow mine.

prādeśikāḥ: 'of limited scope' (chosen, given te'pi 'they too'). The Tibetan phyogs gcig tu, 'partially, in one respect', supports a sense of partial or limited capacity rather than 'of a certain region'.

Rativajra verse: the Tibetan has 'dod pa'i dngos grub, 'the desired accomplishment', for siddhir aninditā, 'blameless accomplishment', and makes 'treasury of all accomplishments' a separate question ('where is the treasury…?'). It also construes the title as an agent (ra ti badzra gyis kyang) where the Sanskrit has the locative rativajre, 'in the Rativajra'. I translate the Sanskrit.

praṇidhipreritāvatāraṇārthaṃ: 'to lead them in, as his vow impelled him'. The Tibetan renders avatāraṇa with gdon pa, 'to draw out, rescue', the word it also uses for samuddharaṇa just before. 'For the sake of a descent (into the world) prompted by his vow' is another possibility.

Nandā, Bhadrā, Jayā, Riktā and Pūrṇā are the five classes of lunar days, kept as names; the Tibetan translates them (dga' ba, bzang po, rgyal ba, stong pa, gang ba: 'joyful, good, victorious, empty, full'). ayam in ayamatyarthaṃ … abhihitaḥ is taken as Rāhu/Kāla. atyartham, 'exceedingly', is now 'expressly', close to the Tibetan khyad par du, 'especially'.

Other Tibetan renderings checked. stimita is brlan, 'moistened', so I now render ānandastimita 'steeped in joy' (stimita means both 'still' and 'moist'; previously 'stilled in joy'). cittaṃ hi is sems nyid, 'the mind itself', which I now follow (previously 'this mind'). Not affecting the reading: mṛgāṅka is calqued as ri dgas mtshan, 'deer-marked'; rāga is glu'i gdangs and Paṭamañjarī is half transliterated as pa Ta ha'i snye ma; Sampuṭodbhavatantrarāja is saM puT 'byung ba'i rgyud kyi rgyal po; yuganaddha is zung 'jug bcings pa, rendering naddha twice.

segments.translit:
diṭakarītyādi| anenopāśakasaṃvarādyanupūrvvā yathā paripāṭyābhiṣikto yogivaraḥ samayasaṅketadravyāpahāreṇa sadgurumārādhyārddharātrau prajñājñānābhiṣeka[ṃ] labdhvā dṛḍhaṃ yathā bhavati| tathā mahāsukhaṃ caturthānanda[ṃ] tvaṃ parimāṇaya|
bhaṇai lui ityādi| tasmin kuliśāravindasaṃyogākṣarasukhopāyaṃ (sukhoya) śrīgurūn pṛṣṭvā viramānande vyāpyavyāpakatayā sarvvadharmmā[3]nupalambharūpaṃ sahajānandamahāsukhaṃ aharniśaṃ jānīhi|
tathāca śrīsamāje—
na vinā vajraguruṇā sarvvakleśaprahāṇakaṃ|
nirvvāṇañca padaṃ śāntamavaivarttikamāpnuyāt||
tathāca nāgārjjunapādaiḥ vajrajāpe coktaṃ—
girīndramūrddhnaḥ prapatettu kaścit
neccheccyutiṃ hi cyavate tathāpi|
guruprasādāptahitopadeśaḥ
icchenna mokṣañca tathāpi muktaḥ||
sarahapādairapyuktaṃ prabandhe—
yā sā saṃsāracakraṃ viracayati manaḥsanniyogātmahetoḥ
sā dhīryasya[āḥ] prasādāddiśati nijabhuvaṃ svāmino niṣprapañca[ṃ]|
tacca pratyātmavedyaṃ samudayati sukhaṃ kalpanājā(ma)lamuktaṃ
kuryyāt tasyāṃhriyugmaṃ śirasi savinayaṃ sadguroḥ sarvvakālaṃ||
śrīhevajre'pi—
ātmanā jñāyate puṇyāt guruparvvopasevayā|
segments.translation:
'Make it firm', and so on. By this he means that the excellent yogin who has received [empowerment]{abhiseka} step by step in due order, in the sequence that begins with the lay vows, pleases the true [guru]{guru} with an offering of the [pledge]{samaya} substances agreed by sign and receives the wisdom-knowledge [empowerment]{abhiseka} at midnight, in such a way that it becomes firm. In the same way, you should take the measure of [great bliss]{mahasukha}, the fourth [joy]{ananda}.
'[Lūyī]{p-luyi} says', and so on. In that state, having asked the glorious [guru]{guru} about the means to the imperishable bliss of the union of [vajra]{vajra} and lotus, know day and night, in the [joy of cessation]{viramananda}, the [great bliss]{mahasukha} of [innate joy]{sahajananda}, whose form, by way of pervaded and pervader, is the non-apprehension of all phenomena.
And so in the glorious [Guhyasamāja]{tx-guhyasamaja}:
Without the [vajra]{vajra} [guru]{guru} one cannot reach
the state that removes all [afflictions]{klesa}, or [nirvāṇa]{nirvana}, peaceful and beyond turning back.
And so the venerable [Nāgārjuna]{p-nagarjuna} has said in the [Vajra]{vajra} Recitation:
Should someone fall from the summit of the king of mountains,
though he does not wish to fall, he falls all the same;
one who has gained helpful [instruction]{upadesa} by the [guru]{guru}'s grace,
though he does not wish for liberation, is liberated all the same.
The venerable [Saraha]{p-saraha} too has said in a composition:
The intellect that, joined with the mind, fashions the wheel of [saṃsāra]{samsara} for its own sake,
that same intellect, by his grace, points to the lord's own ground, free of elaboration,
and there arises that bliss, to be known by each within, free of the net of concepts:
at all times, with humility, one should place on one's head the two feet of that true [guru]{guru}.
In the glorious [Hevajra]{tx-hevajra} too:
It is known by oneself, from merit, by attending on the succession of [gurus]{guru}.
segments.note: Munidatta reads the refrain as addressed to the yogin who, having received the wisdom-knowledge [empowerment]{abhiseka} at midnight, must make it firm and take the measure of [great bliss]{mahasukha}, the fourth [joy]{ananda}. Asking the [guru]{guru} is learning the way to the bliss of [vajra]{vajra}-and-lotus union, and then knowing [innate joy]{sahajananda} day and night. His quotations make the guru indispensable.

citations.quoted: na vinā vajraguruṇā sarvvakleśaprahāṇakaṃ … (Without the vajra guru …)
girīndramūrddhnaḥ prapatettu kaścit … (Should someone fall from the summit of the king of mountains …)
citations.work: Nāgārjuna, Vajrajāpa ('Vajra Recitation'), named as the source; probably the Vajrajāpakrama, first chapter of the Pañcakrama

citations.quoted: yā sā saṃsāracakraṃ viracayati … (The intellect that … fashions the wheel of saṃsāra …)
citations.work: Saraha, an unnamed composition (prabandha); a Sanskrit verse in sragdharā metre, not one of the Apabhraṃśa dohās

citations.quoted: ātmanā jñāyate puṇyāt guruparvvopasevayā (It is known by oneself, from merit …)

flags.note: samayasaṅketadravyāpahāreṇa: apahāra 'removal, theft' gives no sense; I read upahāra 'offering'. The Tibetan (dam tshig gi brda'i rdzas kyis bla ma dam pa mnyes par byas nas, 'having pleased the true guru with the pledge-sign substances') has no word for either, but nothing in it suggests removal.

Structure of the first gloss, revised: following Shastri's daṇḍa after bhavati and the Tibetan, which ends a sentence there (… thob pa ji lta ba bzhin du brtan par bya'o, 'should be made firm, just as it was obtained') and opens the next with de bzhin du, I take the first sentence as glossing 'make it firm' and tathā … parimāṇaya as glossing 'take the measure of great bliss'. The Tibetan reads the second as a statement, bde ba chen po dga' ba bzhi pa nyid kun gyi tshad ma'o, 'great bliss, the fourth joy itself, is the measure of all', taking parimāṇa as a noun; the Sanskrit tvaṃ parimāṇaya is an imperative, which I keep. The nominative yogivaraḥ with absolutives is loose; I turn the absolutives into finite verbs.

kuliśāravindasaṃyogākṣarasukhopāyaṃ (sukhoya): Shastri's parenthesis probably records the manuscript. The Tibetan has … mi 'dzag pa'i bde ba'i phyir, 'for the sake of the non-leaking bliss', with no word for 'means', which points to sukhāya, 'for the bliss', a reading the manuscript's sukhoya may conceal. I translate Shastri's text ('about the means to the bliss'). The Tibetan also renders akṣara as mi 'dzag pa, 'not leaking', the tantric sense of bliss without emission; 'imperishable' may be too abstract.

viramānande (locative, 'in the joy of cessation') appears in the Tibetan as khyad par gyis dga' ba, with an instrumental ('through the special joy'). khyad par gyi dga' ba is, I believe, one of the Tibetan names for the third joy, so this is probably not a different word; the case difference would make the joy the means of knowing rather than its setting. The Tibetan also has an indicative (shes so, 'one knows') for jānīhi, 'know!'.

anenopāśakasaṃvarādy-: the Tibetan has dge ba'i bshes gnyen gyis sdom pa la sogs pa'i rim pas, 'through the sequence of vows and so on, by the spiritual friend', probably a Tibetan slip for or expansion of dge bsnyen, 'lay follower' (upāsaka); I keep 'the lay vows'. śrīgurūn is plural, surely honorific; tasmin, 'in that state' (Tibetan de la), has no stated referent.

Guhyasamāja verse, revised: I now take sarvvakleśaprahāṇakaṃ … nirvvāṇañca as coordinate objects ('the state that removes all afflictions, or nirvāṇa'), as the ca suggests and as the Tibetan does (nyon mongs ma lus spangs pa dang/ zhi ba myang 'das go 'phang dang/ phyir mi ldog pa, listing three), rather than merging them as before.

Saraha's verse, line 2: Shastri restores yasya[āḥ] (feminine), but the correlative tasya … sadguroḥ in line 4 requires masculine yasya, 'by whose (the guru's) grace'; the Tibetan's de yi zhabs zung, 'his two feet', beside bla ma dam pa, also ties the feet to the guru. I translate yasya.

Saraha's verse in the Tibetan, lines 1-2: line 1 has a negative the Sanskrit lacks (gang zhig 'khor ba'i 'khor lo mi sgrub na, 'whoever does not produce the wheel of saṃsāra'), which undoes the Sanskrit's point that the same intellect that makes saṃsāra reveals the lord's ground. In line 2 it has zhugs, 'enters', for diśati, 'points to' (perhaps reading viśati, a common d/v confusion), and dang ba, 'clarity, faith', for prasāda. I translate the printed Sanskrit.

Saraha's verse, revised: for manaḥsanniyogātmahetoḥ the Tibetan bdag nyid ched du yid ni nyer sbyor, 'applying the mind for one's own sake', takes ātmahetoḥ as the idiom 'for one's own sake', so I now render 'joined with the mind … for its own sake' (previously 'yoked to the mind as its cause'). samudayati is intransitive, and with the Tibetan skye 'gyur, 'arises', I now render 'there arises that bliss' (previously 'brings forth a bliss').
Saraha's verse, line 3: kalpanājā(ma)la. The sragdharā metre requires kalpanājāla, 'net of concepts', and the Tibetan rtog pa'i dra ba, 'net of concepts', confirms it. I translate jāla.

Hevajra half-verse, guruparvvopasevayā, revised: the Tibetan bla ma'i rim pa nyer bsten (printed nyer bstan), 'attending on the succession of gurus', takes parvan as 'stage, succession', so I now render 'the succession of gurus' (previously 'the guru at the proper times'). A slip for gurupādopasevayā, 'serving at the guru's feet', remains possible. The Tibetan quotes the same half-verse and no more, so the quotation probably ended there in Munidatta's text.

nāgārjjunapādaiḥ vajrajāpe coktaṃ: the Tibetan rdo rje'i bzlas pa las gsungs, 'said in the Vajra Recitation', treats vajrajāpa as a title, so I now render 'in the Vajra Recitation' (previously 'on vajra recitation'). Renderings that do not change the reading: the Tibetan gives the full name dpal gsang ba 'dus pa for Śrī Samāja, calls the Hevajra dpal dgyes pa'i rdo rje, and renders both vajra (rdo rje bla ma) and kuliśa (rdo rje dang chu skyes) as rdo rje.

segments.translit:
padāntareṇa mahārāganayasamādhyuddīpayannanuśaṃsāmāha|
saala samāhītyādi| bhagavataiva nayabhedenānaṃtāparyyantāḥ samādhayo daśākuśalaparihārāya indriyanirodhāya nirddiṣṭāḥ| tai[3ka]ratra samādhibhiḥ mahārāganaye sukharahitatvāt duṣkarapoṣadhādiniyamaiśca kiñcinna kriyate||
ataḥ śrīsamāje—
duṣkarairnniyamaistīvrairmūrttiḥ śuṣyati duḥkhitā|
duḥkhāddhi kṣipyate cittaṃ vikṣepāt siddhiranyathā|| iti|
tathāca śrīhevajre—
rāgeṇa badhyate loko rāgeṇaiva vimucyate|
viparītabhāvanā hyeṣā na jñātā buddhatīrthikaiḥ||
iti| evaṃ mahāsukhāvaghātena rahitatvena buddhatīrthiko bahūni duḥkhānyanubhūya utpadyante mriyante ca| na te tasya bhāginaḥ|
tathācāgamaḥ—
tattvahīnā na siddhyanti kalpakoṭiśatairapītivacanāt| mahārā[ga]nayacaryyāmapyāha—
śrīsamāje—
pañca kāmān parityajya tapobhirna ca pīḍayet|
sukhena sādhayed bodhiṃ yogatantrānusārataḥ||
tathāca sarahapādaiḥ—
tanutaracittāṅkurako viṣayarasairyadi na sicyate śuddhaiḥ|
gaganavyāpī phaladaḥ kalpatarutvaṃ kathaṃ labhate||
segments.translation:
With the next [verse]{pada}, bringing to light the [samādhi]{samadhi} of the [way of great passion]{maharaganaya}, he speaks in its praise.
'All the [samādhis]{samadhi}', and so on. The [Blessed One]{p-bhagavat} himself, according to the differences between approaches, taught endless, boundless [samādhis]{samadhi} for avoiding the ten non-virtues and for restraining the senses. Here, on the [way of great passion]{maharaganaya}, nothing at all is achieved by those [samādhis]{samadhi}, since they lack bliss, nor by observances such as austerities and the poṣadha fast.
Hence in the glorious [Guhyasamāja]{tx-guhyasamaja}:
Through harsh and arduous observances the body suffers and withers;
suffering distracts the [mind]{citta}, and through distraction [accomplishment]{siddhi} goes astray.
And so in the glorious [Hevajra]{tx-hevajra}:
By passion the world is bound; by passion itself it is freed.
This reversed meditation is not known to Buddhists and [tīrthikas]{tirthika}.
Thus, through the destruction of [great bliss]{mahasukha}, being without it, Buddhists and [tīrthikas]{tirthika} undergo many sufferings, and are born and die. They have no share in it.
And so scripture: 'Those who lack the truth do not succeed, even in billions of aeons.' On the strength of this statement he also teaches the [conduct]{carya} of the [way of great passion]{maharaganaya}, in the glorious [Guhyasamāja]{tx-guhyasamaja}:
One should not give up the five sense pleasures and torment oneself with austerities;
one should accomplish awakening through bliss, following the yoga tantras.
And so the venerable [Saraha]{p-saraha}:
If the tender sprout of the [mind]{citta} is not watered with the pure juices of the [sense objects]{visaya},
how will it become a wish-granting tree that fills the [sky]{gagana} and bears fruit?
segments.note: Munidatta reads the couplet as praising the [samādhi]{samadhi} of the [way of great passion]{maharaganaya}. The countless samādhis taught for avoiding non-virtue and restraining the senses, like austerities and fasts, achieve nothing here, since they lack bliss; with [great bliss]{mahasukha} destroyed, Buddhists and [tīrthikas]{tirthika} suffer, are born and die. Passion itself frees, and awakening is won through bliss.

equations.en: the endless samādhis the Blessed One taught for avoiding the ten non-virtues and restraining the senses

citations.quoted: duṣkarairnniyamaistīvrairmūrttiḥ śuṣyati duḥkhitā … (Through harsh and arduous observances …)
rāgeṇa badhyate loko rāgeṇaiva vimucyate … (By passion the world is bound …)
tattvahīnā na siddhyanti kalpakoṭiśatairapi (Those who lack the truth do not succeed …)
pañca kāmān parityajya tapobhirna ca pīḍayet … (One should not give up the five sense pleasures …)
tanutaracittāṅkurako viṣayarasairyadi na sicyate śuddhaiḥ … (If the tender sprout of the mind …)
citations.work: Saraha; probably a Sanskrit rendering of one of his dohās

flags.note: mahāsukhāvaghātena rahitatvena, revised: the previous draft doubted avaghāta and suggested avagāha. The Tibetan supports the printed text: bde ba rtsa nas bton na bde ba chen po'i de nyid dang bral bas, 'if bliss is uprooted, being without the reality of great bliss'; rtsa nas bton, 'uprooted', renders avaghāta, 'destruction'. I now translate 'through the destruction of great bliss, being without it'. The Tibetan's opening words are its own version of song line 3b ('if bliss is uprooted, one surely dies'), quoted as a lemma, so it treats this sentence as Munidatta's comment on line 3b; the Sanskrit has only evaṃ, 'thus'.

buddhatīrthiko is singular but its verbs (utpadyante, mriyante) and the following te are plural. I take it, as in the Hevajra verse, as 'Buddhists and tīrthikas'. The Tibetan reads the prose differently: sangs rgyas pa'i mu stegs pa rnams, 'the tīrthikas of the Buddhists', i.e. heterodox Buddhists (in the verse it has the ambiguous sangs rgyas mu stegs). That reading would narrow Munidatta's target to Buddhists who behave like tīrthikas.

pañca kāmān parityajya tapobhirna ca pīḍayet: the printed tapobhinna is taken as tapobhir na, and the negative as governing both the absolutive and the verb ('one should not give up the five sense pleasures and torment oneself'). The Tibetan confirms this with two negatives: dka' thub sdug bsngal bsten mi bya/ 'dod yon lnga ni spang mi bya.

anuśaṃsā, revised: the Tibetan has rjes su bsngags pa, 'praise', so I now render 'he speaks in its praise' (previously 'he states its benefit'). mahārāganayasamādhyuddīpayan is irregular (samādhim would be expected), but the sense is clear.

na te tasya bhāginaḥ: I take tasya as great bliss ('They have no share in it'). The Tibetan has de rnams de kho na nyid kyi skal ba dang mi ldan pas, 'they have no share in reality (tattva)', perhaps reading tattvasya; this anticipates the scriptural line on those who lack the truth.

…kalpakoṭiśatairapītivacanāt| mahārā[ga]nayacaryyāmapyāha: the Tibetan (… zhes pa'i tshig las 'dod chags chen po'i tshul gyi spyod pa'ang gsungs te) joins 'from this statement' to what follows, so I now render 'On the strength of this statement he also teaches…' (previously 'for it is said'). The Tibetan also takes duṣkara as a separate item, 'austerities (dka' thub) and fasting (smyung gnas)', which I follow ('observances such as austerities and the poṣadha fast'). Here it renders rāga as 'dod chags; cp.01.m5 has chags pa.

segments.translit:
mahārāganayacaryyārthaniṣyandisākṣātpramāṇānyanyeṣāṃ vita[4]thajñānābhiniviṣṭānāṃ āgrahakhaṇḍanārthaṃ tṛtīyapadamāha|
eṛieu ityādi| paścācchandamoḍḍiyānakaraṇādibandhaṃ vihāya śūnyatāpakṣaketi nairātmadharmmapāśamiti samīpaṃ tadīyāliṅganaṃ kuru| re saṃbodhanaṃ| bho mokṣaśīlāḥ|
tathācāgamaḥ—
etāni tāni śikharāṇi samunnatāni
satkāyadṛṣṭivipulācalasaṃsthitāni|
nairātmabodhakuliśena vidāritātmā
bhedamprayāti sahajairapi duḥkhaśailaiḥ||
segments.translation:
To break the stubbornness of others, who cling to false knowledge, he speaks the third [verse]{pada}: direct proofs that flow from the meaning of the [conduct]{carya} of the [way of great passion]{maharaganaya}.
'Let go', and so on: then, giving up metre and the bonds of practices such as oḍḍiyāna. 'On the side of [emptiness]{sunyata}': the [noose]{noose} is the nature of [selflessness]{nairatmya}; embrace it closely. 'Re' is a form of address: 'O you who are intent on liberation!'
And so scripture:
These are those towering peaks
that stand on the vast mountain of the view of a real self.
The self, split by the [vajra]{vajra} of realizing [selflessness]{nairatmya},
goes to pieces, and with it even the inborn mountains of suffering.
segments.note: Munidatta takes the couplet as breaking the obstinacy of those clinging to false knowledge. One gives up metre and the bonds of practices such as oḍḍiyāna; the [noose]{noose} is the nature of [selflessness]{nairatmya}, to be embraced closely (so the Tibetan translation divides his gloss); 're' addresses those intent on liberation. A quoted verse has selflessness shatter the self.

equations.en: metre (chanda), and the bonds of practices such as oḍḍiyāna
the nature of selflessness (nairātmadharma), the noose to be embraced closely
a vocative: 'O you who are intent on liberation'

citations.quoted: etāni tāni śikharāṇi samunnatāni … (These are those towering peaks …)

flags.note: nairātmadharmmapāśamiti samīpaṃ, revised. The previous draft divided nairātmadharma | pāśam iti samīpam, 'pāsa means near' (Old Bengali pāsa can mean 'side, beside', as Bengali pāśe). The Tibetan reads stong nyid phyogs zhes pa ni bdag med pa'i chos ni zhags pa ste de la 'dir nye bar 'khyud par gyis shig, ''the side of emptiness': the dharma of selflessness is the noose; embrace it closely here', taking pāśa as 'noose' and samīpaṃ as 'closely' with the embrace. I now follow the Tibetan, which agrees with the draft of line 4b. The 'near' reading remains possible and would leave Munidatta glossing no noose.

mahārāganayacaryyārthaniṣyandi-: 'flowing from the meaning of the conduct…'. The Tibetan has chags pa chen po'i tshul gyis spyod pa'i don mi 'dzags pa mngon du gyur pa ni tshad ma'o, 'the meaning of conduct in the way of great passion, non-leaking and made manifest, is the proof', with a negative the printed Sanskrit lacks. It apparently read -ārthāniṣyandi- (a-niṣyandi, 'not flowing out', i.e. without emission), a difference of one vowel sign. I translate the printed text.

paścācchandamoḍḍiyānakaraṇādibandhaṃ, revised: chanda can be 'desire' (previous draft) or 'metre' (chandas). The Tibetan has sdeb sbyor drug, 'the six metres', where Shastri prints paścāc chandam, which supports 'metre' (as does the draft of line 4a) and suggests its text read ṣaṭ, 'six', for paścāt, 'then'. For oḍḍiyānakaraṇādibandha the Tibetan has g.yo sgyu byed pa la sogs pa bcing ba, 'bonds such as practising deceit', perhaps a different reading (kapaṭa-?) or a guess. oḍḍiyāna is probably the yogic 'lock' (uḍḍiyāna-bandha), one of the bodily techniques (karaṇa); kept in source form. pāṭera āsa is not glossed.

nairātmadharma is marked as selflessness (nairatmya) and rendered 'the nature of selflessness', as in the glossary entry noose. The Tibetan bdag med pa'i chos (not the goddess name bdag med ma) supports the doctrinal sense over Nairātmā. dharma could also be rendered 'teaching' or 'reality'.

Quoted verse, vidāritātmā, revised: the Tibetan bdag med rtogs pa'i rdo rjes bdag 'jig cing, 'the vajra of realizing selflessness destroys the self', reads ātmā as 'the self', so I now render 'The self, split by the vajra…' (previously 'Its body split…'). sahajair api: the Tibetan has lhan skyes, its usual word for the technical 'innate', but here the word describes the mountains of suffering as inborn; I render 'inborn' and leave it unlinked to sahaja.

tṛtīyapadam, 'the third verse', appears in the Tibetan as rkang pa gsum, 'three verses', without the ordinal (contrast rkang pa bzhi pas in cp.01.m6); probably a Tibetan slip. sākṣātpramāṇāni stands loosely beside tṛtīyapadam as a second object of āha (the Tibetan makes it a sentence of its own); taken in apposition. The Tibetan renders re as kye'i and mokṣaśīlāḥ as thar pa'i ngang tshul, as expected.

segments.translit:
caturthapadena yathābhūtadharmmyamāhātmyadṛṣṭapratyayatāmāha—
bhaṇai ityādi|—ādisiddhācāryyalūyīpāda evaṃ vadati, mayā lūyīpādena siddhācāryyeṇa dhyānavaseneti| manovijñāne viṣayendriyavalayatvāt| śrīgurau caturthopadeśalabdhābhyāsena yuganaddharūpaṃ dṛṣṭaṃ|
tathā cāgame—
indriyāṇi svapantīva manontarviśatīva ca|
naṣṭaceṣṭa ivābhāti kāyaḥ satsukhamūrcchitaḥ||
dhavanaṃ śaśiśuddhyālinā cavaṇaṃ raviśu[4ka]ddhyā kālinā tadubhābhyāmāsanaṃ kṛtvā svadevatāhaṅkāropaviṣṭaḥ san sākṣāt kṛtaṃ|
tathāca dvikalpe—
ālikālisamāyogo vajrasattvasya viṣṭaraṃ iti||1||
segments.translation:
With the fourth [verse]{pada} he speaks of the conviction that comes from having seen the greatness of reality as it truly is.
'Says', and so on. The first [siddha]{siddha} master, the venerable [Lūyī]{p-luyi}, says this: 'by me, the [siddha]{siddha} master [Lūyī]{p-luyi}, through the power of meditation'; for in mental consciousness the [sense objects]{visaya} and the senses are dissolved. Through practising the fourth [instruction]{upadesa}, received from the glorious [guru]{guru}, the form of [coupled union]{yuganaddha} was seen.
And so in scripture:
The senses seem to sleep, and the mind seems to enter within;
the body, swooning in true bliss, looks as if all its movement were gone.
The [dhamaṇa]{dhamana} is [āli]{ali}, through the purification of the [moon]{moon}; the [camaṇa]{camana} is [kāli]{kali}, through the purification of the [sun]{surya}. Making a seat of the two, and seated in the pride of being his own deity, he realized it directly.
And so in the [Hevajra]{tx-hevajra}:
The union of [āli]{ali} and [kāli]{kali} is the seat of [Vajrasattva]{p-vajrasattva}.
segments.note: Munidatta hears [Lūyī]{p-luyi} testify to what he saw through the power of meditation: [coupled union]{yuganaddha}, reached by practising the fourth [instruction]{upadesa} received from the [guru]{guru}. He reads [dhamaṇa]{dhamana} and [camaṇa]{camana} as [āli]{ali} and [kāli]{kali}, with the purification of the moon and the sun; seated on these two in the pride of his own deity, Lūyī realized it directly.

equations.en: the form of coupled union, seen through practising the fourth instruction received from the guru
āli, through the purification of the moon
kāli, through the purification of the sun
a seat (āsana) made of the two

citations.quoted: indriyāṇi svapantīva manontarviśatīva ca … (The senses seem to sleep …)
ālikālisamāyogo vajrasattvasya viṣṭaraṃ (The union of āli and kāli is the seat of Vajrasattva)

flags.note: manovijñāne viṣayendriyavalayatvāt: valaya 'ring, enclosure' gives little sense; I read vilaya 'dissolution'. The Tibetan supports this: yid dang rnam shes yul dbang thim gyur, 'mind and consciousness, objects and senses, dissolved'. It takes mind and consciousness as a pair among the things dissolved, where the Sanskrit locative makes mental consciousness the place of dissolution; I keep the Sanskrit construal.

Munidatta writes dhavana and cavaṇa for the song's dhamaṇa and camaṇa; I used the glossary forms. The Tibetan's lemmas are zla ba, 'moon', and nyi ma, 'sun', matching its version of line 5b, which has moon and sun in place of the two words; it glosses the moon as dkar po ri bong 'dzin pa, 'the white hare-holder', and the sun as 'od zer stong ldan, 'the thousand-rayed', each purified, as āli and kāli. The identification is the same. The instrumentals śaśiśuddhyālinā / raviśuddhyā kālinā could also be construed 'the seat is made of dhavana by means of āli…'.

sākṣāt kṛtaṃ (Tibetan mngon sum du byas pa'o) is an impersonal passive with no expressed object; I supply 'he' and 'it' (coupled union, from the preceding sentence). śrīgurau (locative) is rendered 'received from the glorious guru', as the Tibetan dpal gyi bla ma'i bzhi pa'i man ngag thob also takes it.

yathābhūtadharmmyamāhātmyadṛṣṭapratyayatām: rendered 'the conviction that comes from having seen the greatness of reality as it truly is'. The Tibetan (ji lta ba bzhin du gyur pa'i chos kyi bdag chen po mthong ba'i rkyen) takes pratyaya as 'condition' (rkyen): 'the condition for seeing the greatness of reality as it is'; it renders māhātmya literally as bdag chen po. dharmmya may be an error for dharma.

The quoted verse differs in the Tibetan: it puts the body's swoon in bliss first and ends sems ni sems med gsal bar snang, 'the mind clearly appears mindless', where the Sanskrit has the body looking as if its movement were gone. The Tibetan also renders the preceding prose on what Lūyī saw as three lines of verse. I translate the Sanskrit.

The closing ||1|| marks the end of the commentary on song 1 and is not translated. The Tibetan writes ādisiddhācārya as dang po sgrub pa'i slob dpon (sgrub, 'practice', for grub, probably a slip) and translates the title Dvikalpa as brtag pa gnyis pa.

questions: Name forms: to follow the glossary rule I rendered Munidatta's Kṛṣṇācārya as Kāṇha, Śrī Samāja as Guhyasamāja, Dvikalpa as Hevajra, and his spellings dhavana and cavaṇa as dhamaṇa and camaṇa. Should the commentary keep his own forms, with them added to the glossary as variants?

kāla: 'Death' hides Munidatta's link between Kāla (whom he identifies with Rāhu) and the kālāgni, 'fire of time', of Kāṇha's verse (cp.01.m2). The Tibetan pulls both ways: its commentary reads kāla as 'time' (de nyid kyi dus su) and kālāgni as dus kyi me, while its song line 1b puts Rāhu (sgra gcan) in place of kāla. Would 'Time', or keeping 'Kāla', serve better? I left 'fire of time' unlinked because it is not the approved English.

Noose or near (cp.01.m5): I have switched to the Tibetan's division of Munidatta's gloss, 'the noose is the nature of selflessness; embrace it closely', which matches the new draft of line 4b and the noose entry. The previous 'pāsa means near' (Old Bengali pāsa, 'side') is still possible. Please confirm, since it decides whether Munidatta glosses a noose at all.

Line 4a: Munidatta gives chanda for chāndaka, which the Tibetan reads as 'the six metres' (sdeb sbyor drug), and 'the bonds of practices such as oḍḍiyāna' (probably the yogic lock) for bāndha karaṇaka, where the Tibetan has 'bonds such as practising deceit'. He does not gloss pāṭera āsa. This may bear on the draft's 'hope in the rules of practice'.

Blessed One (cp.01.m2): I kept 'the Blessed One's five stages'; the Tibetan makes the Blessed One the one who ripened the practitioners' virtue. If the Tibetan construal is preferred, the glossary definitions of p-bhagavat and pancakrama, which speak of 'the Blessed One's five stages', need changing.

Five branches (cp.01.m2): rūpādayaḥ pañcaskandhāḥ implies, without saying so, that the five branches are the five aggregates; the Tibetan lacks 'five' and folds the aggregates into what is taken as the body-tree. Should the first symbolic reading in the taruvara entry be softened?

Buddhists and tīrthikas (cp.01.m4): the Tibetan prose reads buddhatīrthika as 'the tīrthikas of the Buddhists' (heterodox Buddhists). The tirthika entry says 'most likely Buddhists and tīrthikas', which I followed. Which should the commentary use?

lotus: I left 'lotus' unlinked in 'lotus feet' and 'lotus mouth' (m1, m2) and in 'the union of vajra and lotus' (m3), because the lotus entry describes the flower of song 10. Should the vajra-lotus union link to it, or have its own entry?

First-gloss terms (siddha, vajra, rāga, samādhi, bodhicitta, āli, kāli, dhamaṇa, camaṇa): the weave schema has no field for a first-occurrence gloss, so I relied on the glossary links. Is a gloss wanted inside the woven notes?

Emendations: I translated emended readings where the printed text gave no sense: acyuti to cyuti (m2) and valaya to vilaya (m6), both now supported by the Tibetan; apahāra to upahāra (m3), on which the Tibetan is silent; yasyāḥ to yasya (m3), consistent with the Tibetan. I kept the printed avaghāta (m4), which the Tibetan supports, and Shastri's prākṛ[ta] (m2) and sukhopāyaṃ (m3), which the Tibetan does not reflect. Should the commentary follow emendations or the printed text, with the alternative in a note?
